title: A Fistful of Paintballs (1)

jokes.text: Opening chase scene: 'I see you, chubby ass!' / 'I ain't chasing, chubby.' / 'Chubby-chaser.' — taunts escalating while Fat Neil runs
jokes.setup: Cold open drops us into a paintball chase with no context; someone is being taunted while running
jokes.punchline: The taunter escalates from 'chubby ass' to 'fat-ass' to being called a 'chubby-chaser' — the insult bouncing back ironically
jokes.explanation: Functional cold-open energy. The 'chubby-chaser' reversal is a minor wordplay beat but the insult-as-joke relying on Fat Neil's weight is a bit cheap. It establishes tone more than it earns laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Fat Neil
dialogue.line: Hey! Come back here!

dialogue.speaker: Unknown pursuer
dialogue.line: You can't run forever, Neil! I can see you from space!

dialogue.speaker: Fat Neil
dialogue.line: That's not even geographically accurate!

dialogue.speaker: Unknown pursuer
dialogue.line: Neither is your diet!

jokes.text: "There's only one rule, Fat Neil. The prize goes to the last man standing. So to speak."
jokes.setup: Villain lays out the rule menacingly, then realizes Annie (a woman) is present
jokes.punchline: "So to speak" — an awkward, belated gender correction that deflates his tough-guy speech
jokes.explanation: Tight economy — the two-word add-on does the entire comedic work. The villain's tough-guy posturing instantly crumbling over a small social correction is a solid structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So Fat Neil, you need to understand the paintball rules. You're going to be running around a lot, so to speak.

jokes.text: "If you were a dude, I'd have my fist up your balls."
jokes.setup: Villain is trying to threaten Annie after she disarms him
jokes.punchline: His attempted menace produces an anatomically absurd and unintentionally homoerotic threat that makes no logical sense
jokes.explanation: The threat is so malformed it loops around to being funny — 'fist up your balls' is anatomically nonsensical in a way that undercuts his menace perfectly. Good economy, decent originality for a villain throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: I'm gonna rip off your face and use it as a mask.

jokes.text: Annie disarms the antagonists, then corrects one who reaches for a gun: "Christina 'Reach-y', I said kick."
jokes.setup: Annie is in full action-hero mode, commanding the disarmed antagonists
jokes.punchline: She instantly invents and deploys a sarcastic nickname ('Reach-y') as if it's already this person's established identity
jokes.explanation: Very Annie — she's hyper-competent and slightly unhinged with authority. The on-the-spot nickname deployed with total calm authority is a sharp character joke. It tells you everything about who she is in this episode in three words.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Nobody reach for a gun.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why would we reach for a gun?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because I'm about to say something crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What if we all just... left?

jokes.text: "You gotta learn to trust people." — Jeff to Annie after she refuses to leave enemies armed
jokes.setup: Annie is being ruthlessly pragmatic in a paintball warzone
jokes.punchline: Jeff, of all people — the show's most self-interested character — lectures Annie about trusting people, in the middle of a war game
jokes.explanation: Jeff's hypocrisy is the joke, and it works because the show has earned it. The character integration is high — this line only works coming from Jeff. Functional rather than brilliant.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We played D&D together as friends!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That doesn't mean anything. We have paintball wars.

jokes.text: "We're friends, Annie. Remember? We played Dungeons & Dragons together." / "That was a game." / [beat] / "This is paintball."
jokes.setup: Neil desperately invokes their shared history (the Season 2 D&D episode) to appeal to Annie's mercy
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat "That was a game" / "This is paintball" distinction — delivered with total seriousness — is a magnificent non sequitur that equates the two activities while insisting they're different
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the cold open and one of the episode's best. The structure is impeccable — a beat between the two lines lets the absurdity land. It callbacks a beloved episode, Annie's delivery of the distinction as if it's perfectly logical is funnier than any elaborate joke, and the economy is near-perfect. The joke earns its 8+ because Annie is treating paintball with more moral gravity than a game that was literally played to save someone's life. It's character-rich, structurally tight, and deeply quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Attention everyone, the school picnic is this Saturday at noon. We'll have games, food, and a three-legged race.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh, and Jeff Winger will be demonstrating CPR on an actual cardiac patient. It's really quite educational.

jokes.text: "Free ice cream and that one guy having a heart attack aren't the only surprises today."
jokes.setup: Dean is doing cheerful school announcements at the end-of-year picnic
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions "that one guy having a heart attack" as a fun surprise on par with free ice cream, with zero concern
jokes.explanation: The Dean's cheerful obliviousness to human suffering is pitch-perfect character work. Grammatically, the sentence structure makes the heart attack parallel to free ice cream as a 'fun surprise.' The economy is excellent — it's one clause doing enormous work. Earns its 7+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: This year's paintball prize will be... reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Completely... reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I mean, it's not going to be anything crazy like a... a tank or anything.

jokes.text: Dean builds up excitement about the prize being different from last year ("I've been assured—" with exaggerated enthusiasm), then Pistol Patty announces $100,000 cash
jokes.setup: Dean reassures everyone last year's prize was "way too valuable" and this year will be different
jokes.punchline: The prize is $100,000 cash — objectively MORE valuable and MORE likely to cause chaos than last year's prize
jokes.explanation: Classic Community escalation gag — the show promises to learn from past mistakes and immediately makes the same mistake bigger. The reveal lands well and sets up the entire episode's stakes. Structural comedy at the episode level.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I promise that this year's prize would be more reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The grand prize is... one million dollars!

jokes.text: "I heard a rumor you never shoot an unarmed man." / "Whoever started that rumor didn't eat my beans." / "Then I guess it's lucky for me I'm not unarmed. / Seeing as I'm... eating your beans."
jokes.setup: Classic Western standoff dialogue — Annie approaches the Black Rider with a tough-guy opening line
jokes.punchline: The 'reveal' that she's holding a gun is undercut by the absurd detail that she's also just... eating his beans, making her look both badass and silly simultaneously
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully constructed three-part exchange. The Western genre pastiche is committed and the final beat — the mundane act of eating beans as her 'weapon' — subverts the tough-girl posturing perfectly. It's the episode's genre-parody in miniature: deadly serious framing, absurd payoff. Annie eating his beans while drawing is a visual/comedic concept that earns the 7+ craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You can't shoot an unarmed man. That's not how the West works.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Unless he ate your beans.

jokes.text: "Yeah? And I want pants."
jokes.setup: Jeff's messenger tells Annie that Jeff wants to see her
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat, equal-weight response — equating Jeff's strategic desires with her own unmet need for pants
jokes.explanation: Four words doing maximum work. The joke works on two levels: it's funny as a straight deadpan complaint, and it implies Annie is in a compromised warzone state (pantless) that she's treating with complete pragmatic equanimity. Perfect economy score.

dialogue.line: Reveals they're literally eating the other person's beans

jokes.text: "Math club's gotten a lot better since last year. Obviously, they were practicing while the rest of us went on dates."
jokes.setup: Jeff observes the math club has significantly improved their paintball game
jokes.punchline: His explanation — they were practicing while normal people dated — is both a compliment and an insult, delivered with Jeff's signature effortless condescension
jokes.explanation: This is a Jeff-specific joke — the casual cruelty disguised as neutrality ('while the rest of us went on dates') is perfectly in his voice. Not a standout but functional and character-true.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yeah, well I want pants.

jokes.text: "Hold on. I have a plan. Math club! Yeah. I'm Asian. You guys Asian? / That's pretty racist, man. / That wasn't a no."
jokes.setup: Chang is trying to get the Math Club to let him through their territory
jokes.punchline: His plan: appeal to racial solidarity. When called out as racist, his comeback — "That wasn't a no" — is both logically correct and deeply revealing about his character
jokes.explanation: "That wasn't a no" is a razor-sharp callback within the same exchange. Chang's self-awareness about the racism combined with his complete shamelessness about using it anyway is perfect character comedy — it only works because it's Chang. The structure is tight: accusation → non-defense that is also a correct logical observation.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I want to join the math club. I'm very good at math. I can count to one hundred in my sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Math Club Member
dialogue.line: That's... not really what we do here.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh, I see. You probably want someone more... Asian.

dialogue.speaker: Math Club Member
dialogue.line: What? No, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'm very Asian. I have the highest cheekbones in Greendale.

jokes.text: "Don't shoot me, shoot him. He's white, and he's out of ammo."
jokes.setup: Chang tries to escape Math Club by immediately betraying the person he was just traveling with
jokes.punchline: He provides tactical intel on the person's race and ammunition status as his negotiating chip
jokes.explanation: Chang's immediate betrayal and the specificity of his intel ('he's white') is good character comedy. The escalation from the previous joke (he just invoked Asian solidarity, now he's throwing a white guy under the bus) gives it extra punch.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm joining the math club to expand my horizons and build meaningful friendships.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Actually, I've noticed the Korean student over there has been getting all the problem sets right. I think he's stealing my answers.

jokes.text: "Shoot Chang! He defected to the math club. / Math club! / Agh. / Forget it. Just a waste of ammo."
jokes.setup: Chang dramatically announces his new allegiance
jokes.punchline: The group's reaction: not anger, not conflict — just pragmatic dismissal. He's not worth the paint.
jokes.explanation: Chang's irrelevance to the main group is a running theme. 'Just a waste of ammo' perfectly encapsulates how the study group has always treated Chang — as a nuisance not worth engaging. Solid character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yeah, this is definitely the safest group I've ever been in.

jokes.text: "Yeah, we're running low, too. / Shut up, Abed. / Okay."
jokes.setup: Jeff is in a tense negotiation; Abed helpfully volunteers their tactical weakness
jokes.punchline: Jeff shuts Abed down instantly; Abed accepts this with zero affect
jokes.explanation: Abed's literal-minded helpfulness sabotaging a tense moment is classic — and his one-word 'Okay' acceptance is perfect deadpan. Small joke, well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce has enough ammunition to make a French art student jealous.

jokes.text: "He's a jerk because we exclude him. We exclude him because he's a jerk."
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are having a circular argument about Pierce
jokes.punchline: Annie articulates the chicken-and-egg paradox of their relationship with Pierce with perfect precision — it's comedic because it's true and unsolvable
jokes.explanation: The chiasmus structure makes it quotable and the observation is sharp — it's the most economical summary of the Pierce situation all season. This is the kind of line that makes Community's writing stand out: it's funny AND it's true AND it advances theme in six words.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, you can't just do whatever you want because you're rich.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because it's wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: But I'm rich.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's circular logic.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know. That's how I got rich.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That doesn't make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, it's the perfect metaphor for this group. We're trapped in circular logic.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We stay together because we're together. We're friends because we're a group. We're a group because we're friends.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is we're stuck.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Sounds like my marriages.

jokes.text: "Okay, I'm-- I am dead now. I'm dead." — Shirley, apparently shot during Jeff and Annie's argument
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are having an earnest emotional argument about Pierce in the middle of a warzone
jokes.punchline: Shirley has been shot and presumably dying while they debate, and she announces it with weary resignation — the argument continues without her
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom rhythm: the emotional conversation continues while something absurd happens to a third character. Shirley's patient repetition ('I am dead now. I'm dead.') as if she needs to be formally acknowledged is excellent. The escalation from 'I'm--' to full commitment works structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Who are you?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Cowboy
dialogue.line: Name's not important.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: Okay, but real talk—spurs? In a paintball game?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Cowboy
dialogue.line: They're thematically appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Abed Nadir
dialogue.line: They're impractical and thematically appropriate.

jokes.text: "Who wears spurs in paintball?" — reaction to Black Rider's entrance
jokes.setup: The Black Rider makes a dramatic entrance, apparently in full cowboy regalia
jokes.punchline: Annie cuts through the genre fantasy with a completely practical question about an absurd wardrobe choice
jokes.explanation: Five words perfectly puncturing the Western fantasy the show is indulging. Annie is the audience surrogate here and the line is clean. High economy score because it does the whole job in one breath.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This mysterious cowboy character just appeared with no explanation. It's like the show's budget suddenly increased.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, are you saying I'm not worth a higher budget?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm saying the cowboy is.

jokes.text: "Does that guy even go to this school? / He's really good-looking. Like, network TV good-looking. / And did you see how big his guns were? / Why don't you just marry him, Abed?"
jokes.setup: The group reacts to the Black Rider's intimidating entrance
jokes.punchline: Abed's commentary escalates from tactical observation to aesthetic appreciation to what sounds like a crush — "network TV good-looking" is a meta joke about the show's own casting standards
jokes.explanation: "Network TV good-looking" is a genuinely clever meta-joke — a community college show poking fun at the unrealistic attractiveness standards of network TV, while itself being a network TV show. Abed delivers it with his characteristic analytical detachment, which makes it funnier. Jeff's jealous 'why don't you just marry him' is a perfect cap. This earns 8 on character integration: only Abed frames attraction as an aesthetic/analytical category.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're deputies now. We have authority.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We can stop you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Over what? A two-block radius of a community college parking lot?

jokes.text: Troy and Abed's reunion: "I thought you were dead." / "I thought you were dead." — mirrored exchange, then immediately snap to business
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed encounter each other after separation in the warzone
jokes.punchline: Their perfectly synchronized exchange — same words, same beat, same emotional flatness — followed by immediate pivot to deputizing the group
jokes.explanation: The mirrored dialogue is on-brand for Troy and Abed — their friendship exists in a slightly different reality where they are always in sync. The charm is entirely in character integration. Functional but warm.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My forehead isn't too big, right?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's huge.

jokes.text: "Deputies? What are you, Deputies of the Stairwell?" / "Fort Hawthorne."
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed announce themselves as 'deputies' with full gravity
jokes.punchline: The reveal that there's an actual fort named 'Fort Hawthorne' — implying Pierce has built a whole Wild West settlement in the school — lands as pure absurdist escalation
jokes.explanation: The two-word punchline 'Fort Hawthorne' is doing a lot — it promises something both absurd and very Pierce-specific. Good economy and structure for a world-building reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce set up a whole humanitarian effort in the fort. He's got water stations, first aid kits, blankets...

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What about sleeping arrangements?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, he's got cots, sleeping bags, pillows—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And a bed for me with Egyptian cotton sheets, a down comforter, and a little bell so someone can bring me warm milk before I sleep.

jokes.text: "There's a bounty on your head, my friend. / Pierce. / My forehead's not that big, right? / [beat] It's not small."
jokes.setup: Troy tells Jeff there's a bounty on his head; Jeff is mentally stuck on the wrong meaning
jokes.punchline: Pierce's insecurity about his forehead size emerges from nowhere, and Britta's diplomatic non-denial ('It's not small') makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection: 'bounty on your head' → 'my forehead's not that big.' The beat and Britta's response are what elevate it. 'It's not small' is the perfect non-answer that answers everything. Earns its score through structure and that devastating Britta cap.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, why do we keep calling him 'The Cowboy'? He's not actually wearing a cowboy hat or boots or anything cowboy-related.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, he's terrorizing us like a cowboy would.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But that's not what a cowboy is! A cowboy is a specific occupation involving cattle herding in the American West. By that logic, we should call him 'The Guy' because he's a guy!

jokes.text: Troy: 'Mm.' / Abed: 'It's not small.' [responding to Pierce asking if his forehead is big]
jokes.setup: Pierce asks if his forehead is big
jokes.punchline: Troy's uncomfortable 'Mm' (a non-answer) followed by Abed's diplomatic but damning 'It's not small' — the most precise possible non-confirmation that it IS in fact large
jokes.explanation: 'It's not small' is a genuinely excellent line — the most economical possible way of confirming something is large without saying it. Abed's deadpan precision turns what could be a throwaway into a quotable moment. The double-beat structure (Troy's 'Mm' then Abed's line) is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It all started in a bathroom. I realized people have a desperate need for basic bathroom access. That's when I knew I had found my empire.

jokes.text: "He's created a safe zone where people can rest, eat, and if necessary, pump their breast milk."
jokes.setup: Troy is describing Fort Hawthorne's amenities to sell Jeff on surrendering
jokes.punchline: The list escalates to breast milk pumping — a completely unexpected and oddly specific amenity that reveals the fort has become a full civilization
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of amenities ending with breast milk pumping is a classic 'rule of three' subversion — rest, eat, and then something completely unexpected. The specificity ('if necessary') makes it funnier. Troy delivering this with complete sincerity as a selling point is high-impact absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not a monster. You guys are my friends. Free bathroom privileges for all of you.

jokes.text: "Oh, and your drugs."
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed list the terms of surrender: hand over your guns
jokes.punchline: The casual afterthought addition of 'your drugs' implies someone in the group has drugs on them — delivered with zero judgment or elaboration
jokes.explanation: The 'oh, and your drugs' throwaway works because it's never explained. The implication is funnier than any elaboration would be. Good economy — the joke is exactly as long as it needs to be.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I got entertainment more your speed, Jeff. It's called Gaywatch.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Not yet. But when it is, you're gonna love it.

jokes.text: "It began with a dream, Annie. A dream and an impulse to hide in the men's room. I found that people were willing to roll bullets under the door, just for the right to take a dump."
jokes.setup: Pierce is grandly explaining how he built Fort Hawthorne
jokes.punchline: His empire began in a bathroom stall — he discovered he could monetize toilet access in a paintball warzone, which is both capitalist genius and deeply gross
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It earns 8+ because it's pure Pierce — his entrepreneurial instinct, his complete lack of shame, and the absurdist logic all combine into something that could ONLY be him. 'A dream and an impulse to hide in the men's room' is structurally beautiful: the epic framing ('a dream') immediately deflated by the cowardly truth. 'Roll bullets under the door for the right to take a dump' is an economy of comedic concept that generates both laughs and world-building simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, she needed the Twinkies and I needed to see her dance. It's called a mutually beneficial arrangement, Jeffrey.

jokes.text: "By the way, for you guys, taking a dump's on the house." Pierce's hospitality offer
jokes.setup: Pierce is welcoming his study group to Fort Hawthorne with regal generosity
jokes.punchline: His most prestigious gift to his friends is free bathroom access — an absurd callback to his bathroom economy that reveals what his version of VIP treatment looks like
jokes.explanation: Direct callback to the bathroom economy that lands because Pierce is sincere about this being a generous offer. His complete blindness to how low a bar this is makes it funnier than the original joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Summer means different things to different people. For some, it's a time to travel, to explore new places. For others, it's about spending time with family and friends. But for me? Summer is just... a long, empty stretch of time where I sit alone in my house, waiting for September when I can come back here and pretend I have a life.

jokes.text: "Or if you prefer, relax and catch a show." — Pierce gestures toward an entertainer (implied to be Vicky dancing for Twinkies)
jokes.setup: Pierce is showing off Fort Hawthorne's entertainment amenities
jokes.punchline: He has set up a performer — later revealed to be a dance major dancing for Twinkies — as his court entertainment, completely unconscious of the exploitation
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the Vicky/Twinkie reveal later. Works as a visual suggestion of Pierce's inadvertent feudalism.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We need to pump.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we really need to pump.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pump? Like... like at the gym? You guys want to go to the gym?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No, Troy. We need to pump. You know, express milk.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh. OH. I... I didn't... I'm gonna go.

jokes.text: "Because you're gay." — Pierce to Jeff, apparently bringing over a male companion
jokes.setup: Pierce says he has someone 'more your speed' for Jeff — implying a woman
jokes.punchline: The punchline is that Pierce's version of a compliment to Jeff is to assume he's gay (and presumably bring him a man), which is both homophobic and weirdly affectionate in the Pierce way
jokes.explanation: Very Pierce, but the gay joke itself is the weakest link — the show has used this gag before. It's rescued somewhat by Pierce's sincerity and Jeff's immediate 'I think I've seen enough.' Below-average earned_vs_cheap because it leans on a tired Pierce crutch.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Mr. Chang, you stand accused of infiltrating Greendale Community College under false pretenses.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Your Honor, those are just pretendsies.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: Did he just say pretendsies?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Yes, your Honor. He did.

jokes.text: "Ah, the twinkies are wonderful tonight."
jokes.setup: Pierce is hosting dinner in Fort Hawthorne with exaggerated aristocratic flair
jokes.punchline: He delivers a wine-tasting-style appreciation of Twinkies — treating gas station snacks as fine dining — which is both absurdist and an Eric Clapton 'Wonderful Tonight' parody
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Pierce's oblivious aristocratic self-delusion. The line works as a standalone non sequitur and as a parody of fine dining culture. Economy is excellent — he's playing Clapton's romantic dinner as a Twinkie supper. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! I have something to confess!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I told the football team that you guys said their uniforms make them look fat!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And I may have mentioned that you think the mascot costume smells like old cheese and regret!

jokes.text: "Ah, the twinkies are wonderful tonight."
jokes.setup: Pierce is hosting the study group for dinner in his paintball fort
jokes.punchline: He delivers a formal dinner compliment — 'the twinkies are wonderful tonight' — as if they're at a fine restaurant, treating Twinkies as a cuisine
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. 'The twinkies are wonderful tonight' is funny on multiple levels: (1) it's a parody of refined dinner party small talk applied to the most undignified food, (2) it perfectly captures Pierce's delusion about his own status, (3) the construction is a direct parody of Eric Clapton's 'Wonderful Tonight' in its phrasing, which adds a musical joke layer. The economy is perfect — nine words that fully establish an absurd world.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I... I think I have beans at home that need... watering?

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: Beans don't need watering, they need soil.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not a botanist!

jokes.text: "Give us some space, Miguel."
jokes.setup: Pierce has enlisted locals as his Fort Hawthorne staff
jokes.punchline: He casually dismisses someone named 'Miguel' — the nonchalance implies he has an entire serving staff and has already memorized their names, suggesting a fully realized feudal micro-society in a school building
jokes.explanation: One throwaway line that tells you Pierce has built an entire fiefdom. The specificity of the name 'Miguel' (a named underling!) is the joke — it implies a whole world. Pure character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Do you go to school here?

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: No, I'm a professional paintball player.

jokes.text: "I'm not risking my butt hauling ammo back for the guy that has Vicky dancing for twinkies. / She's a dance major, Jeff. And she loves twinkies."
jokes.setup: Jeff objects to Pierce's exploitation of a student dancing for snack food
jokes.punchline: Pierce's defense — she has a relevant degree AND she enjoys the payment — is both completely missing Jeff's point and somehow also a reasonable argument, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce logic — he's simultaneously terrible and making a coherent point. 'She's a dance major and she loves twinkies' as a complete ethical defense of exploitation is the kind of joke that only works in Pierce's mouth. The character integration is very high: the same defense from anyone else wouldn't land. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: That gun's emptier than your head, sweetie.

jokes.text: Pierce's speech: "For you guys, it means pool parties, dinners, one-night stands. For me... It means counting down the days 'til next fall."
jokes.setup: Pierce is making an emotional appeal for the group to help him
jokes.punchline: The humor lies in the pathos — Pierce's summer is so empty he literally counts down to community college, while everyone else has actual lives. It's funny and devastating simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Community at its best: a joke that's also a genuine emotional beat. The list structure (pool parties, dinners, one-night stands) versus the deflation of 'counting down the days' is structurally clean. Earns its high character integration score because this is the most Pierce Pierce has ever been — his loneliness made briefly visible.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: He's not that mysterious. He just wore all black and didn't talk much.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So he was basically a teenager going through a phase?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Exactly. Also, he kept dropping his sword and picking it back up.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Threatening. Really threatening.

jokes.text: "More juice, Miguel."
jokes.setup: Pierce has just finished toasting with the study group
jokes.punchline: He immediately summons Miguel again — the named attendant returns, cementing that Pierce has actual staff in his paintball fort
jokes.explanation: The callback to Miguel earns additional laughs by confirming the joke. 'More juice, Miguel' is funnier than the original because now we know Miguel is a real presence, not a one-off gag. The regal casualness of juice service in a paintball fort.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're not good-looking AND you're not a good shot? What exactly do you bring to the table?

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I'm very mysterious.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're not even that mysterious. You keep telling us stuff.

jokes.text: "I hope we find this cache of ammunition soon. I need to pump. / Me, too. / You talkin' about peeing, right? / No. / Me, neither."
jokes.setup: Shirley mentions she needs to pump; Jeff assumes urination
jokes.punchline: Both women confirm they mean breast pumping, leaving Jeff isolated in his naivety
jokes.explanation: Callback to the breast milk pumping amenity and a decent misdirection gag. The structure is clean, Jeff's isolation is well-played. The 'me neither' from Annie is the unexpected escalation — Shirley yes, Annie less obvious. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, how did you even survive that?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce told me where you'd be. He said he wanted to help, but then he just... left me there.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce betrayed you?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I know. I can't believe I trusted him. Again.

jokes.text: "Benjamin Chang, for your betrayal of the Cheerleaders' Alliance, I sentence you to pretendsies death. / Ready... / I'm sorry I told Trish about Amber! / Aim... / Fire."
jokes.setup: Chang faces mock execution by the Cheerleaders' Alliance for betrayal
jokes.punchline: During his last-second confession ('I'm sorry I told Trish about Amber!'), the squad fires mid-drama — the execution continues through the interpersonal drama, treating both with equal absurd gravity
jokes.explanation: The cheerleader drama within the execution structure is a good bit — 'pretendsies death' is an excellent term — but the Trish/Amber subplot is too undefined to fully land. The genre pastiche (formal execution) is well-committed.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I need to get into the storage closet to retrieve the paintball supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no, no, no. The key is in there, and I'm going to have to... squeeze in to get it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: This is... this is very confined. Very intimate. With the shelving.

jokes.text: "I'm sorry I told Trish about Amber!" — Chang's desperate last confession
jokes.setup: Chang is facing the firing squad and desperately tries to appeal to individual cheerleaders
jokes.punchline: His confession is specific, personal, and implies a whole soap-opera backstory — he tried to find the one person he could hurt to save himself
jokes.explanation: Chang weaponizing cheerleader drama as a last-ditch survival tactic is very Chang. The specificity of 'Trish' and 'Amber' makes it funnier — it implies a whole world of cheerleader intrigue that we don't need to know about.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going in. I need to look confident, powerful, and above all else, attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because if I'm going down, I'm going down looking like I could've won.

jokes.text: "Holy crap. / Not cool, bitch. / Yeah, so you told me at last year's tryouts."
jokes.setup: Chang is shot; a cheerleader is indignant
jokes.punchline: 'Not cool, bitch' as a reaction to being shot in paintball — and the follow-up implying the person has heard this before — treats a paintball shooting as a social violation with long-term history
jokes.explanation: The 'you told me at last year's tryouts' is a small gem — implies rich backstory and ongoing social grievance. Functional episode texture.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff, you literally just said you'd abandon us for a pretty girl on a motorcycle.

jokes.text: "Can I join you? / No! / Okay."
jokes.setup: After being shot and left by both alliances, Chang asks to join the people who just shot him
jokes.punchline: He's rejected instantly, accepts it completely without protest
jokes.explanation: Chang's endless social rejection with zero self-awareness is a running gag. The speed of the exchange (three syllables) is its best quality. High economy.

jokes.text: "I'm the bad guy. / Stop trying to fluster me with your handsomeness. You're creepy. / Then why is your chest getting all flushed? / It's a rash. I'm allergic to beans."
jokes.setup: Black Rider confronts Annie; she tries to maintain composure against his attractiveness
jokes.punchline: "It's a rash. I'm allergic to beans" — Annie's physiological response to his hotness is explained away with a perfectly absurd medical excuse that also callbacks her earlier bean-eating
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'I'm allergic to beans' works as a callback (she ate his beans), as a denial of attraction, and as a character beat about Annie being unable to admit weakness. The structure — his perceptive challenge met with an increasingly specific medical lie — is tight. The specificity of 'beans' as the allergen is the comedic perfection: it's not 'I have a rash,' it's 'I'm ALLERGIC TO BEANS,' which is both more defensive and more absurd. Earns 8+ on character integration: only Annie deflects attraction this way.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, if you must know, I was just making sure they were blanks. Last season, someone kept loading real bullets and I wasn't about to let that happen again.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, that was you.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Exactly. So I learned my lesson.

jokes.text: Annie threatens "I'll hit you in the foot" and Black Rider responds "Thank you."
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to threaten the Black Rider but is out of ammo; he calls her bluff
jokes.punchline: His 'Thank you' — accepting what would normally be a threat as a gift — reveals he's so confident he's treating her worst option as a favor
jokes.explanation: Two words doing maximum work. 'Thank you' as a response to 'I'll hit you in the foot' is perfect deadpan — it acknowledges the threat, processes it, and dismisses it entirely in a single gracious phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We haven't excluded you, Pierce. You're always welcome to hang out with us.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh really? Then why wasn't I invited to game night last Tuesday?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because you said you had a prostate exam.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I rescheduled it! And nobody told me about cards night either.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That was literally yesterday. We texted the group chat.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I don't check that thing. My fingers are too big for the phone.

jokes.text: "You're dry, sugar."
jokes.setup: Annie attempts to shoot the Black Rider
jokes.punchline: He informs her she's out of ammo with the casual condescension of 'sugar' — equal parts dismissive and weirdly gentlemanly
jokes.explanation: Three words, Western drawl condescension. The 'sugar' is the joke — simultaneously patronizing and weirdly charming in the genre context.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You guys are playing cards without me? What is this, some kind of conspiracy?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, we need to talk about your membership in the group.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We've been voting.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Voting? On what?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: On whether you stay or go.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, you were voting on me this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: The cards were just a cover.

jokes.text: "I'll save you for last." / "You won't get the chance."
jokes.setup: Classic villain/hero Western exchange
jokes.punchline: The exchange is so genre-perfect it's comedic in its earnestness — two people playing out a Western while covered in paint
jokes.explanation: Genre pastiche exchange. Functions as texture rather than a standalone joke — the commitment to Western genre is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, someone voted to keep Pierce?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: One person did.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Who would do that?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, obviously it was me.

jokes.text: "I got a better look at him. He's not that good-looking. / Didn't he shoot you? / He tried. / He's a bad shot, too? / Man, what does this guy have going for him?"
jokes.setup: Jeff encounters the Black Rider; Troy asks what happened
jokes.punchline: Jeff, clearly rattled by the attractive rival, insists the guy isn't good-looking and is a bad shot — both provably false. Troy's 'What does this guy have going for him?' is a perfect straight-man puncture of Jeff's delusion.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's vanity is the show's most reliable joke, and this is a peak execution. The character integration earns 9 because the insecurity is so specifically Jeff — only he would claim the clearly superior fighter is 'not that good-looking' and 'a bad shot' after getting beaten. Troy's straight-man delivery of 'What does this guy have going for him?' is devastating because Troy is sincerely baffled. The callback structure (Abed praised the guy at length earlier) makes it land harder on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: Your hair isn't real, is it?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No, it's... it's real.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I can tell by the way it moves. It's a wig.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's not a wig!

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: You're bald underneath. That's why you're so angry.

jokes.text: "Pierce loaded your gun with blanks."
jokes.setup: Jeff survived the encounter with the Black Rider and is boasting/confused
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Jeff's survival was not skill but Pierce's sabotage — his gun had blanks
jokes.explanation: Clean structural reveal that retroactively recontextualizes Jeff's earlier bravado and sets up Annie's confrontation with Pierce. Good economy and plot-comedy integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, you've faked a heart attack before. Remember when you pretended to have a stroke so you wouldn't have to go to that diversity seminar?

jokes.text: "Don't--don't--don't shoot! / Why does this keep happening?"
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton is encountered in the warzone
jokes.punchline: His resigned 'Why does this keep happening?' implies this is a recurring personal catastrophe — he's so accustomed to Greendale chaos that he's developed a running complaint about it
jokes.explanation: The Dean's weary relationship with Greendale chaos is a reliable source of character comedy. 'Why does this keep happening?' as his catchphrase-in-formation is good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It worked! It actually worked!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I can't believe you all fell for it. You're all idiots.

jokes.text: "And what kind of ice cream company does this?"
jokes.setup: Annie surveys the Greendale warzone created by the ice cream company's promotional game
jokes.punchline: The question is a perfect articulation of the show's meta-absurdism: a legitimate business question that highlights how insane the premise is
jokes.explanation: Good observational beat that also foreshadows the conspiracy reveal. Annie being the voice of reasonable outrage is well-characterized.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I don't go to school here.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: You've got a face like a foot and a butt for a brain.

jokes.text: "The key's in my shorts." / [pause] / "I can get it out, I guess."
jokes.setup: Jeff needs the key to the weapons locker; Dean has it on his person
jokes.punchline: The Dean's "I can get it out, I guess" — with evident reluctance/disappointment that Jeff isn't more enthusiastic — is classic Dean innuendo with plausible deniability
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean — the joke is in what he doesn't say. 'I can get it out, I guess' implies he was hoping Jeff would volunteer. The character integration is very high: this is entirely about the Dean's unrequited thing for Jeff. The beat between the two lines does the comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I have to go. My shift at Kinko's starts in twenty minutes.

jokes.text: "Okay, Black Rider. Now let's see who's attractive."
jokes.setup: Jeff arms himself from the cache and prepares to face the Black Rider
jokes.punchline: Jeff's battle cry is about attractiveness, not winning — his main motivation is the existential threat to his hotness, not the prize money
jokes.explanation: "Now let's see who's attractive" as a WAR CRY is an all-time Jeff line. The character integration earns a 9: no one else on this show would phrase battle preparation this way. It's the perfect crystallization of Jeff's entire character arc in the episode. The payoff of building up his insecurity about the Black Rider's looks for fifteen minutes before this line makes it land hard. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I'm not a student. I never was.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? Then who are you?

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: Let's just say the ice cream sponsorship was never really about ice cream.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. How deep does this go?

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: Deeper than you can imagine. And if you're smart, you'll forget you ever saw me.

jokes.text: "Dude, you have a problem."
jokes.setup: Jeff delivers his 'let's see who's attractive' war cry
jokes.punchline: Troy, deadpan, tells Jeff he has a problem — both a reaction beat to Jeff's line and a perfect one-sentence character observation
jokes.explanation: Four words serving as the audience surrogate. Troy as the voice of gentle disbelief is well-deployed here. The economy score is high because there's no better way to cap that joke.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I'm leaving this important conspiracy.

dialogue.speaker: Black Rider
dialogue.line: I have to go to a Nickelback concert.

jokes.text: "Agh! Okay, okay, okay!" — Pierce confessing to loading Jeff's gun with blanks when confronted by Annie
jokes.setup: Annie confronts Pierce about the blanks; we see her apparently threatening him physically
jokes.punchline: Pierce's instant capitulation ('Okay okay okay!') under Annie's intimidation — the most imposing member of the group being the tiniest one — is a physical comedy beat inferred from his reaction
jokes.explanation: Annie intimidating Pierce is well-established character comedy — she's the most ruthless person in the group when motivated. His triple 'okay' is the perfect capitulation rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown invader
dialogue.line: Your pitiful resistance is as ineffective as your general education requirements.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown invader
dialogue.line: We have conquered worse academic institutions.

jokes.text: "Oh, I get it. So once again, I'm the bad guy."
jokes.setup: Pierce has been caught sabotaging Jeff's gun; Annie confronts him
jokes.punchline: Pierce's self-pitying 'So once again I'm the bad guy' — when yes, he objectively is the bad guy — is delivered with total genuine grievance, as if this is an unfair pattern
jokes.explanation: Annie's flat 'Yes' makes this. Pierce's obliviousness to his own villainy while feeling victimized by being called a villain is a sharp character beat. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: Are we like the Little Rascals?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was a Little Rascal.

jokes.text: "Put it in your holster. / Come on, Annie. You're my favorite. I don't wanna beat you. / It's just that I don't want Jeff to be-- / Put the gun in your holster, and let's play the game. / Right. So you can shoot me and play without me. / [beat] That's this group's favorite thing."
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to claim he's letting Annie go because she's his favorite
jokes.punchline: "That's this group's favorite thing" — Pierce's self-pity crystallizes into an accusation that is both petty AND accurate, with the beat before it letting the weight land
jokes.explanation: The pivot from Pierce being magnanimous to Pierce being wounded is structurally excellent. The beat before 'That's this group's favorite thing' lets the audience catch up. It's character work in the guise of a punchline — and it sets up the vote revelation. Character integration is very high because this is Pierce at his most human.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, I guess we're all going to hell.

jokes.text: "We weren't playing cards. We were voting, and you weren't invited because we were voting about you."
jokes.setup: Pierce accuses them of playing cards without him three days ago
jokes.punchline: Britta, unable to filter herself, blurts out the truth — they were voting on whether to keep Pierce in the group — which is both more hurtful than cards AND reveals Britta's complete lack of social tact
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta — she means to defend the group but makes it infinitely worse. The joke is that her 'correction' of Pierce's assumption reveals something far more damaging. The character integration is excellent: only Britta would blurt this out in this context. The dark comedic beat of the vote revelation is structurally perfect setup for the red card payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You think you're so smart, Jeff, but you're about to learn what it's like when you mess with Pierce Hawthorne.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Is that a threat, Pierce?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's not a threat, it's a promise. You're going to hell in a handbasket on an iceberg.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's how mad I am — I'm breaking the laws of metaphor!

jokes.text: Pierce: 'That's this group's favorite thing.'
jokes.setup: Pierce accuses the group of shooting him (metaphorically) and playing without him
jokes.punchline: 'That's this group's favorite thing' — his self-pity crystallized into a single ironic line that is both a joke and a genuine indictment
jokes.explanation: One of Pierce's most effective lines — it functions as bitter humor but also lands emotionally. 'That's this group's favorite thing' is the kind of line that gets a laugh and then sits with you. Strong economy, perfect character voice.

jokes.text: "Lucky for you, it had to be unanimous. There was one holdout. One red card."
jokes.setup: The vote revelation has just landed; Annie deepens the wound
jokes.punchline: The reveal that someone voted to keep Pierce — but we're left to infer who — is both a cliffhanger and a joke about how close Pierce came to ejection from his only social circle
jokes.explanation: The 'one red card' reveal is structurally elegant — it's simultaneously Pierce's salvation and his humiliation (he almost didn't make it back). The withholding of who held out is the right call: the ambiguity is the joke. Dark comedy that earns its impact.

jokes.text: Pierce picks up and stares at the red card in silence — the moment lands as an anti-joke beat
jokes.setup: Pierce has just learned one person voted to keep him in the group
jokes.punchline: His silence as he processes this information — and the audience's uncertainty about whether he's touched or devastated — is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Non-verbal comedy at its best — the silence is doing more work than any line could. Pierce's stillness is the culmination of his season arc and the episode's emotional thread. The humor comes from the cringe of the group watching him process it. Earns its score on character integration and economy.

jokes.text: "Black Rider... It's Jeff Winger. I know you've heard of me by now. / No."
jokes.setup: Jeff steps forward to parley with the Black Rider, invoking his own name as if it's famous
jokes.punchline: "No." — Instant deflation. The Black Rider has no idea who Jeff is.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Jeff's entire identity is built on the assumption that he's the most important person in every room. The setup — 'I know you've heard of me by now' — is perfectly Jeff-sized ego. The single-word 'No' is a perfect structural punchline: minimal, devastating, complete. The character integration earns 9 because this joke only works as a Jeff joke — his name-dropping of himself. It's the episode's funniest single beat and among the most quotable lines in the series.

jokes.text: "Starting with you, Mr. Insecure. You think you're good-looking, but you're not. You're average. You're just an average-looking guy with a big chin."
jokes.setup: The Black Rider agrees to the truce, then immediately attacks Jeff's appearance
jokes.punchline: He targets Jeff's specific vulnerability — the entire episode's through-line — and the 'big chin' is a callback to Jeff's forehead insecurity earlier, now displaced onto another feature
jokes.explanation: "Average. You're just an average-looking guy with a big chin" is a devastating callback to Jeff's entire episode arc of appearance anxiety. The specificity of 'big chin' (a real Joel McHale feature) makes it land harder. Earns its score through character integration and the callback payoff.

jokes.text: Pierce's fake heart attack sequence: group debates whether it's real while he 'gurgles'; Jeff insists it's fake; "The gurgling's a nice touch"; Pierce reveals it was fake: "Sucker!"
jokes.setup: Pierce apparently collapses; group debates whether to call 911
jokes.punchline: Jeff's detached 'The gurgling's a nice touch' followed by Pierce's triumphant 'Sucker!' when it's confirmed fake — but the reverse twist is that Jeff was RIGHT and the group that believed him looks foolish
jokes.explanation: "The gurgling's a nice touch" is a highlight — Jeff's total refusal to be emotionally manipulated while everyone else panics. The escalating doubt, the specific 'gurgling' critique, and 'Sucker!' as the reveal work together. The sequence has good structural arc: threat → doubt → critique → confirmation → triumph.

jokes.text: "Last week he did it to get out of letting me have a stick of gum."
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why he knew Pierce's heart attack was fake
jokes.punchline: Pierce has apparently faked a heart attack before — over a single stick of gum — which retroactively reveals a pattern of calculated manipulation over trivial stakes
jokes.explanation: "A stick of gum" as the previous fake-heart-attack trigger is a genuinely surprising specific detail that makes Pierce's villainy funnier than it has any right to be. The disproportion between 'heart attack' and 'stick of gum' is the comedic engine. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: "The gurgling's a nice touch."
jokes.setup: Pierce is gurgling dramatically during his fake heart attack
jokes.punchline: Abed critiques the performance quality while Pierce is 'dying' — clinical appreciation of the production value of a fake medical emergency
jokes.explanation: Five words of pure Abed. 'The gurgling's a nice touch' treats Pierce's fake death as a performance review — Abed is critiquing the craft of the fake-out rather than reacting emotionally. Only Abed would do this. The detached appreciation while everyone else is horrified or suspicious is a perfect character moment. Very high economy and character integration scores are both justified.

jokes.text: "You guys are terrible people." — after Pierce fakes a heart attack and shoots someone
jokes.setup: Some group members correctly identified the heart attack as fake; others believed it; both sides argued passionately
jokes.punchline: Annie's 'you guys are terrible people' is directed at the people who correctly called the bluff — moral condemnation of being right
jokes.explanation: Annie's misplaced moral outrage is character-true but not a standout beat — the real laugh is in Pierce's 'Sucker!' The Annie follow-up reinforces the irony but doesn't add much.

jokes.text: "You're the worst. / I'm the best! / We've created a monster. / Let's not give ourselves too much credit."
jokes.setup: Pierce has triumphed with his fake heart attack gambit
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Let's not give ourselves too much credit' — refusing to claim responsibility for Pierce — is a perfect character cap. Pierce has always been this way; they didn't make him.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-distancing from Pierce is both a character joke and an episode-level observation. 'Let's not give ourselves too much credit' deflates the 'we created a monster' cliché while making a point about Pierce's pre-existing condition. Good economy.

jokes.text: "I'm out. Some old guy pretended to have a heart attack. Shot me in the gut. I don't care. That's your problem. This school sucks."
jokes.setup: The Black Rider has been eliminated; Annie encounters him leaving
jokes.punchline: His complete detachment — not angry, just done — and 'This school sucks' as his professional assessment of Greendale is both a straight man's reaction and the audience surrogate
jokes.explanation: The Black Rider's exit is well-played. His total lack of dramatic grievance — 'I don't care. That's your problem.' — is funnier than any outburst would be. 'This school sucks' is a perfect outsider verdict on Greendale.

jokes.text: "Well, then why do you go here? / I wouldn't go to this toilet with my big sister's toe. / I take a class online. / I was paid to be here and win the game so my boss could keep his prize money."
jokes.setup: Annie asks why he attends Greendale if he hates it
jokes.punchline: The conspiracy reveal — he was a hired ringer — is both a plot escalation and a great joke about Greendale's reputation. "I wouldn't go to this toilet with my big sister's toe" is an inspired insult.
jokes.explanation: "I wouldn't go to this toilet with my big sister's toe" is an oddly specific and highly quotable insult — the precision of 'big sister's toe' elevates it above a standard 'this place sucks' line. The conspiracy reveal following it is well-structured: answer the question, undermine it, reveal the twist.

jokes.text: "We've created a monster." / "Let's not give ourselves too much credit."
jokes.setup: Pierce has just stormed off declaring victory
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'we've created a monster' treats Pierce as their responsibility; Abed's correction — 'let's not give ourselves too much credit' — implies Pierce was always going to be a monster regardless
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'Let's not give ourselves too much credit' deflates the idea that they made Pierce bad — implying he was factory-preset this way. It's both a great Abed line (clinical, honest) and a genuinely insightful character observation. The economy of the exchange is excellent.

jokes.text: "I got Coldplay tickets." as his reason for leaving
jokes.setup: Black Rider is explaining why he's leaving despite the game still going
jokes.punchline: His reason for abandoning a $100,000 game is Coldplay tickets — both a mundane deflation of the high-stakes drama and a mild diss of Coldplay as a priority
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of Coldplay — a band associated with mild-mannered mainstream sentimentality — as the thing that beats out $100,000 is well-chosen. It characterizes the Black Rider as someone who takes his personal plans seriously regardless of stakes. Good deadpan.

jokes.text: "Too late, bean allergy. You blew it."
jokes.setup: Annie tries to get information about the conspiracy after he's decided to leave
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'bean allergy' — using her earlier excuse against her as a nickname, and 'You blew it' as a final dismissal
jokes.explanation: "Bean allergy" as a departing nickname is a perfect callback payoff — he heard her lie, remembered it, and weaponizes it as a farewell. The economy is excellent: two words do the entire job of saying 'I know you were lying, I know you like me, and I'm gone.' Earns high marks on callback structure.

jokes.text: "Hello? Anybody? Does anyone have an alliance I can join? I'm really loyal." — Chang, alone
jokes.setup: Chang has been abandoned by every faction in the game
jokes.punchline: His lonely plea for an alliance — emphasizing his loyalty despite having betrayed every alliance he's joined — is both pathetic and oblivious
jokes.explanation: "I'm really loyal" after a full episode of betrayals is the perfect cap to the Chang subplot. The irony is total and the character integration is excellent — Chang genuinely believes this about himself. His isolated 'Hello? Anybody?' in an empty hallway is a good visual/audio joke.

jokes.text: "No Greendale student can be allowed to win this game. Initiate plan B: Operation Total Invasion."
jokes.setup: The conspiracy is revealed — the ice cream company was rigging the game
jokes.punchline: 'Operation Total Invasion' as the ice cream company's military operation name — the escalation from cowboy-themed promotional contest to full corporate paramilitary strike
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — the comedic concept of an ice cream company having a 'Plan B: Operation Total Invasion' is appropriately absurd. Sets up the finale well.

jokes.text: "Resistance is as pointless as your degrees."
jokes.setup: The ice cream company's forces address the Greendale students over a PA
jokes.punchline: The condescending aside about community college degrees — from a corporate entity that has just launched a military operation over a paintball game — is a perfect absurdist escalation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a dig at community college, it's absurd coming from an ice cream company, and it's the perfect villain monologue flourish. The economy is excellent — the aside about degrees is unexpected but perfectly placed. Earns its high impact score.

jokes.text: "Are we the little rascals? / I was."
jokes.setup: The students are pinned down and outnumbered — Troy makes a pop culture reference to describe their underdog situation
jokes.punchline: Abed's literal 'I was' — confirming he actually was one of the Little Rascals (or played one) — delivered mid-crisis as if this is a relevant clarification
jokes.explanation: "I was" is a perfectly Abed two-word joke. His matter-of-fact confirmation during a crisis moment is exactly his character — mid-action he's doing a brief autobiographical clarification. The economy score is 9 because nothing else is needed. High character integration: only Abed would have been in a Little Rascals reboot AND prioritize this correction now.

jokes.text: "Are we the little rascals?" / "I was."
jokes.setup: The group is being overrun; Troy looks around at their ragtag team
jokes.punchline: "I was" — Abed confirms he was indeed playing 'the little rascals' as a character role this whole time, delivered as a matter-of-fact revelation
jokes.explanation: One of the best Abed lines in the episode. 'I was' answers the question in a way that reframes everything — Abed has been consciously playing a Little Rascals character this whole time, which is both completely in character (he lives life as genre performance) and a perfect meta-joke about the show's ensemble dynamics. The two-word answer is devastating in its confidence. High marks across the board, especially character integration and economy.

jokes.text: "I'm on your team! Stop shooting me!" — Chang, running through the final battle
jokes.setup: The invasion begins and all hell breaks loose
jokes.punchline: Chang is apparently being shot by his own team — his irrelevance has escalated to friendly fire
jokes.explanation: Chang's running rejection gag reaches its natural endpoint: his own team shoots him. Functional running gag payoff but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "I had a dream it would end this way. / Once I'm gone, I'm gone. / Then I guess I'll see you in hell. / That's just the tip of the iceberg."
jokes.setup: The group is being overrun in what appears to be their final stand
jokes.punchline: The sequence of increasingly dramatic last-words declarations — culminating in Abed's completely inexplicable 'That's just the tip of the iceberg' as his dying words — is a comedic escalation of soap-opera finality
jokes.explanation: "That's just the tip of the iceberg" as final words is a great Abed non sequitur — it implies a much larger Abed reveal that will never come. The escalating melodrama of everyone's last words works as an episode-closing joke about the show's genre awareness.

tmdb_overview: A $100,000 paintball war prize pits members of the study group against one another, until they decide to join forces to stop a mysterious challenger.
insight: Western parody anchors 55 jokes across 45 minutes, though setup-heavy structure prevents higher impact.
